reference_title: Design, Analysis, and Testing of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations that Support Transportation Facilities
chapter_title: Design Process and Team Roles for Analysis of Laterally Loaded Deep Foundations

sections.title: Design Process
sections.summary: The design procedure (Figure 5-1), lateral loading only, is a logical sequence that is iterated in practice: Blocks 1 to 17 run from project type, performance criteria and design-build requirements through geotechnical conditions, loads, investigation, characterization, foundation type, layout and head fixity, trial size, single-pile limit states (9.1 to 9.4), axial design, group analysis, structural design, constructability, documents, cost, construction and reporting.
sections.body: The chapter outlines the design procedure for laterally loaded deep foundations and the roles of geotechnical and structural engineers, for lateral loading only (driven piles, drilled shafts, CFA piles and micropiles in general: Hannigan et al. 2016, Brown et al. 2010, Brown et al. 2007, Sabatini et al. 2005). The step-by-step procedure often does not follow a linear path: project size, contracting and loading complexity change the order, with iterations for new data, design changes or constructability. It is illustrated in Figure 5-1 (pp. 49 to 50), with design-build roles and overlap shown conceptually; roles vary by project. Block 1, project type, performance and constraints: (1) the structure (new or replacement bridge, retaining or noise wall, slope stabilization, sign or light post); (2) site conditions affecting type and lateral loading (right-of-way, access, overhead constraints, scour, construction over water, waves or vessel impact, wetlands, adjacent structures, vibration limits); (3) layout, grades, surficial characteristics, geology; (4) special events (seismic, scour, downdrag, vessel impact); (5) preliminary loads, even order of magnitude; (6) load and resistance factors for Strength, Service and Extreme Event, global stability resistance factors reflecting consequences of failure (Section 4.6) (p. 48); (7) performance criteria (limiting deflection, maximum factored resistance, global stability). Sometimes deep foundations with controlling lateral loads are known early (noise walls, excavation support, slope stabilization); sometimes not, as for a bridge where rock or dense soils are shallow. Block 1a, design-build (p. 51): the owner sets performance requirements before tender (specifications, investigation requirements, lateral design procedures, maximum resistance factors, minimum lateral load testing, inspection and testing), deviations from AASHTO such as site-specific p-y geologic models or deflection criteria, and may specify or preclude foundation types; the design-builder will use the maximum resistance factor allowed unless tied to other criteria. Block 2, preliminary geotechnical conditions: a desktop study to find poor soils, IGMs, rock type and depth and precedent (load tests, performance records, PMT or DMT data, local practice), informing the investigation; in design-build a baseline investigation may be done here. Block 3, applied loads from a preliminary layout, axial and lateral (axial load influences lateral performance), with load combinations and factors (Chapter 4) (p. 52). Block 4, investigation and testing, possibly staged; foundation locations are often not final at the initial investigation. Block 5, stratigraphy, groundwater and parameters for lateral analysis, which may differ from those for axial analysis. Block 6, foundation type: lateral capacity, lateral soil displacements, constructability, adjacent structures, low headroom, noise and vibration, local contractors, project size, corrosivity, work over water; it needs experienced judgment, axial capacity may control, and it may be iterated (p. 53). Block 7, initial layout and head fixity: spacing may reduce soil resistance through shadowing (Chapter 7), often refined later; free head for single or isolated piles/shafts, fixed head for multiple rows. Block 8, trial size and depth and a subsurface profile per load case (p. 54) including variability, scour, liquefied layers, new fill and compression of soft layers; scour is assessed for the design flood (typically 100-year, Strength and Service) and the check flood (up to 500-year, Extreme Event), and alters the profile rather than the loads or factors. Block 9, single pile analysis for Geotechnical Strength, Structural Strength, Service and Extreme Event: head deflection and rotation, maximum moment and shear, nominal moment resistance (plastic hinge), including axial loads; lengths by trial (some programs give length versus deflection); trial longitudinal reinforcement about 1 percent of the shaft area for drilled shafts or CFAs (Brown et al. 2010; Brown et al. 2007). Block 9.1, Geotechnical Strength with factored lateral and axial loads, several combinations if none is clearly critical or profiles differ (scour, extreme event). Block 9.2 (p. 55), Structural Strength: nominal axial, shear and flexural resistance must exceed the factored effects (Brown et al. 2010); otherwise add reinforcement, a heavier steel section or a larger size, re-checking geotechnical strength (Chapter 11). Block 9.3, Service: actual tolerable deformation in final design, including amplification above the foundation (pier columns, wall tops), sometimes set by aesthetics; a soil-structure interaction method such as p-y is required, results kept distinct from strength runs. Block 9.4 (p. 56), Extreme Event, resistance factor 0.80: check flood scour, earthquakes, ice, vessel and vehicle collision. Block 10, axial design: minimum penetration is the greatest of that for axial design, for lateral loads and for settlement (axial design is not in this manual). Block 11 (p. 57), group analysis for overlapping zones and frame action, by p-multipliers in single pile analysis or group software (Chapter 7), for all limit states. Block 12, final structural design and cap connections (Chapter 11): force effects, dimensions, axial, shear and moment checks, reinforcement and its spacing for concrete flow, connections consistent with the assumed head fixity. Block 13, constructability review (Chapter 13): construction sequence, precluded methods, contractor qualifications, openings in shaft cages, inspection and testing. Block 14 (p. 58), construction documents with minimum tip elevations, installation, testing (lateral load test location, setup, procedures, acceptance criteria, reporting; Chapter 12) and quality control. Block 15, cost estimate. Block 16, construction changes (Chapter 13), best avoided by attention to variability, risk and constructability in design. Block 17, post-construction records; full documentation and publication of load test data are recommended for future projects and resistance factor calibration. Design-build (p. 59): the owner may do exploration, characterization, conceptual type selection, preliminary design and minimum criteria; the design-builder's engineer of record does the final design; some projects are procured after Blocks 1 to 4, others after a preliminary design through Block 14, with Blocks 4 to 14 repeated by the design-builder. (pp. 47 to 59)
key_points: The procedure (Figure 5-1) is iterative and covers lateral loading only (p. 47).
Free head for single or isolated piles/shafts; fixed head for multiple rows (Block 7) (p. 53).
Design flood typically 100-year (Strength, Service); check flood up to 500-year (Extreme Event) (p. 54).
Trial longitudinal reinforcement about 1 percent of shaft area (Block 9) (p. 54).
Service analysis must use soil-structure interaction such as p-y (Block 9.3) (p. 55).
Extreme Event resistance factor 0.80 (Block 9.4) (p. 56).
Minimum penetration: greatest of axial, lateral and settlement requirements (Block 10) (p. 56).
Design-builders use the maximum resistance factor allowed unless tied to other criteria (p. 51).

sections.title: Design Team Roles
sections.summary: The design team is mainly the geotechnical and structural engineers, with hydraulic and civil engineers, architects and others giving secondary input. Lateral analysis is soil-structure interaction, so neither discipline should analyze alone; it needs coordination, often iteration. Roles vary with local practice and contracts.
sections.body: The design team for deep foundations consists primarily of the geotechnical and structural engineers; hydraulic and civil engineers, architects or other disciplines may give secondary input. Because lateral analysis involves soil-structure interaction, it requires their combined expertise: the geotechnical engineer should not analyze without understanding the structural response and the connection to the structure, and the structural engineer should not analyze without understanding how the section, depth or spacing affect the geotechnical response or how external loads such as seismic loads affect the parameters or surrounding soils. Proper design therefore requires adequate coordination, often iteration between the two disciplines rather than one supplying inputs or a check to the other. The typical roles described (5.2.1 to 5.2.3) follow general industry and agency practice and may vary with local practice, contracts or other considerations. (p. 59)
key_points: Team: geotechnical and structural engineers, with secondary input from others (p. 59).
Soil-structure interaction requires both disciplines; often an iterative process (p. 59).

sections.title: Geotechnical Responsibilities in Lateral Loading Analysis
sections.summary: The geotechnical engineer leads subsurface tasks (preliminary conditions, investigation, characterization, resistance factors), external geotechnical loads (earth pressure, slope movement, liquefaction, downdrag), axial design, constructability, inspection and testing, and should lead Broms or strain wedge analyses; p-y analysis may be done by either discipline. Leads on geotechnical projects such as slope stabilization.
sections.body: The geotechnical engineer has primary responsibility for tasks relating to subsurface conditions and secondary responsibility for structural design; some tasks may go to either engineer depending on project type, roles, experience, contracts or other considerations. Subsurface tasks (p. 60): preliminary geotechnical conditions, the investigation and testing program, characterization, and development of resistance factors (based partly on the characterization). The geotechnical engineer also determines external geotechnical loads (retained earth pressure, slope movement, changed soil conditions such as liquefaction, lateral flow or spreading), or provides parameters (unit weight, earth pressure coefficient) for the structural engineer to develop them, plus axial loads such as downdrag and effects such as ground settlement at the foundations; and leads axial design, constructability and construction inspection and testing requirements. On geotechnical projects or where loads are mainly geotechnical (slope stabilization, cantilevered retaining walls), or with unusual conditions or specialty construction, the geotechnical engineer may also lead project definition, type and preliminary size, layout and head fixity, and performance criteria. Single pile analysis may be either discipline's; the geotechnical engineer should lead Broms or strain wedge analyses. The p-y analysis has both inputs: either the geotechnical engineer runs it and the structural engineer reviews it and/or does the Structural Strength analysis, or the geotechnical engineer supplies the profile, parameters and p-y curves or their inputs and the structural engineer runs the Geotechnical Strength and Service analyses. Group analysis software may be run by either. The geotechnical engineer will likely lead the constructability review and the specifications for installation and construction inspection and testing, and may lead plans for geotechnical construction such as slope stabilization or specialty foundations (micropiles, CFA piles) (printed "geotechnicap-yl"); primarily structural plans (bridge pile layout, shaft details) get secondary review. In construction (p. 61) the geotechnical engineer reviews specialty contractor submittals, oversees inspection and testing, approves installation records, leads as-built records on geotechnical projects and otherwise supports them. (pp. 59 to 61)
key_points: Primary for subsurface tasks, resistance factors and external geotechnical loads (p. 60).
Should lead Broms or strain wedge analyses; p-y analysis by either discipline (p. 60).
Leads specifications for installation and construction inspection and testing (p. 60).
Leads design and as-builts on geotechnical projects such as slope stabilization (pp. 60 to 61).

sections.title: Structural Responsibilities in Lateral Loading Analysis
sections.summary: Bridges, walls, noise walls, signs and light poles are structural projects led by the structural engineer: project definition, layout and head fixity, performance criteria (head deflection, shear and moment capacity), applied loads, Structural Strength, structural design and cap connections, documents and as-builts; may also run single pile and group analyses with geotechnical inputs.
sections.body: Most transportation projects (bridges, retaining walls, noise walls, signs, light poles) are primarily structural and led by the structural engineer, who is primarily responsible for structural design tasks: project type and needs, foundation layout and head fixity, performance criteria (allowable deflection at the pile/shaft head and shear and moment capacity), applied loads (structural loads and reactions at the top of the elements), the Structural Strength Limit State, preliminary and final structural design of elements and cap connections, construction documents and as-built records. The structural engineer may also lead design of individual elements and group analysis, including Geotechnical Strength and Service Limit States, using geotechnical inputs, and should take part in the constructability review. For projects that are primarily geotechnical, involve specialty geotechnical construction or unusual conditions ("as discussed in Section 5.3.1", as printed; the discussion is in 5.2.1), the geotechnical engineer may lead with the structural engineer in support, reviewing loads, structural design of elements and connections, layouts and specifications, and construction submittals relating to structural design (load test apparatus set-up, shoring). (p. 61)
key_points: Structural engineer leads most transportation projects: bridges, walls, signs, light poles (p. 61).
Sets performance criteria: allowable head deflection, shear and moment capacity (p. 61).
May run Geotechnical Strength and Service analyses with geotechnical inputs (p. 61).

sections.title: Other Team Members
sections.summary: Hydraulic engineers give hydraulic loads, flood elevations and scour depths; civil engineers site grading that adds unbalanced earth pressure or downdrag; construction engineers check installation against the plans and flag differing conditions. Others may set cost, noise and vibration limits, space limits, contractor availability, procurement method or emergency status.
sections.body: Other team members include hydraulic and civil engineers, architects, construction engineers or other specialties. Hydraulic engineers determine loads from currents and wave impacts, flood elevations and design scour depths. Civil engineers determine site grading that may affect loading, such as cuts or fills causing unbalanced earth pressures (additional lateral loads) or fill causing settlement and downdrag. Construction engineers represent the project during construction, ensure the foundations are installed per the plans and specifications, coordinate with the contractor and alert the designer to differing site conditions or as-built foundations that may affect the design. Architects or other disciplines may determine cost estimates, constructability reviews, noise or vibration threshold limits or space restrictions, and may lead on availability of local contractors or materials, preferred procurement (design-build or design-bid-build) and whether the project is an emergency response, each of which may affect the foundation type. (p. 62)
key_points: Hydraulic engineers: hydraulic loads, flood elevations, scour depths (p. 62).
Civil engineers: grading that adds unbalanced earth pressure or downdrag (p. 62).
Construction engineers flag differing site conditions or as-built foundations (p. 62).

sections.title: Need for Communication and Coordination
sections.summary: Team members must communicate requirements (tolerable deflection, loads, subsurface conditions) and whether values are factored, to avoid assumed or overly conservative values and double factoring; each discipline should review the other's analyses. Early conservatism should be re-assessed; e.g., relaxing a deflection limit may allow a lighter section, and IGM characterized conservatively may cause excessive depths.
sections.body: As discussed in "Sections 5.3.1, 5.3.2, and 5.3.3" (as printed; the roles are 5.2.1 to 5.2.3), team members must communicate and coordinate. Requirements such as tolerable deflections, loading and subsurface conditions must be determined and communicated to avoid assumed or overly conservative values or double application of load and resistance factors; communication should state whether loads and resistances are factored or unfactored/nominal, which factors to apply, and group factors. Individual and group analyses by one discipline should be reviewed by the other to confirm adequacy and find missed improvements; coordination is also needed for plans, specifications, testing requirements and constructability reviews. Early design inputs often carry conservatism (deflection limit, parameters, characterization, foundation size or type, loads) so that refinement does not increase size, depth or number and cost, with the intent that refinement verifies the preliminary design and may allow optimization. Too often disciplines provide conservative but individually reliable criteria and do not re-assess them when the design is complete (p. 63). Without coordination, opportunities are lost: IGM characterized conservatively as stiff or dense soil may give excessive depths, and the geotechnical engineer may not see how the characterization affected the design; or, given a limiting deflection, the geotechnical engineer may find that a heavy section is needed where a lighter one would serve with slightly greater deflection, and should ask the structural engineer whether the criterion can be relaxed. Communication with other disciplines and stakeholders helps too, e.g., micropiles may avoid mobilizing and making access for large cranes at sites with limited access. Geotechnical and structural engineers should coordinate on drawings and specifications and join the constructability review (Section 5.2). (pp. 62 to 63)
key_points: State whether loads and resistances are factored; avoid double application of factors (p. 62).
Each discipline should review the other's single pile and group analyses (p. 62).
Re-assess early conservative criteria once the design is complete (p. 62).
A relaxed deflection limit may allow a lighter, cheaper section (p. 63).
sections.applicability: Multi-discipline project teams; any project where geotechnical and structural engineers collaborate on lateral foundation design
